Abstract Background An inadequate protein intake may offset the muscle protein synthetic response after physical activity, reducing the possible benefits of an active lifestyle for muscle mass. We examined the effects of 12 weeks of daily protein supplementation on lean body mass, muscle strength, and physical performance in physically active older adults with a low habitual protein intake (<1.0 g/kg/day). Methods A randomized double‐blinded controlled trial was performed among 116 physically active older adults [age 69 (interquartile range: 67–73) years, 82% male] who were training for a 4 day walking event of 30, 40, or 50 km/day. Participants were randomly allocated to either 31 g of milk protein or iso‐caloric placebo supplementation for 12 weeks. Body composition (dual‐energy X‐ray absorptiometry), strength (isometric leg extension and grip strength), quadriceps contractile function, and physical performance [Short Physical Performance Battery, Timed Up‐and‐Go test, and cardiorespiratory fitness (Åstrand–Rhyming submaximal exercise test)] were measured at baseline and after 12 weeks. We assessed vitamin D status and markers of muscle damage and renal function in blood and urine samples before and after intervention. Results A larger increase in relative lean body mass was observed in the protein vs. placebo group (∆0.93 ± 1.22% vs. ∆0.44 ± 1.40%, P Interaction = 0.046). Absolute and relative fat mass decreased more in the protein group than in the placebo group (∆−0.90 ± 1.22 kg vs. ∆−0.31 ± 1.28 kg, P Interaction = 0.013 and ∆−0.92 ± 1.19% vs. ∆−0.39 ± 1.36%, P Interaction = 0.029, respectively). Strength and contractile function did not change in both groups. Gait speed, chair‐rise ability, Timed Up‐and‐Go, and cardiorespiratory fitness improved in both groups ( P < 0.001), but no between‐group differences were observed. Serum urea increased in the protein group, whereas no changes were observed in the placebo group ( P Interaction < 0.001). No between‐group differences were observed for vitamin D status, muscle damage, and renal function markers. Conclusions In physically active older adults with relatively low habitual dietary protein consumption, an improvement in physical performance, an increase in lean body mass, and a decrease in fat mass were observed after walking exercise training. A larger increase in relative lean body mass and larger reduction in fat mass were observed in participants receiving 12 weeks of daily protein supplementation compared with controls, whereas this was not accompanied by differences in improvements between groups in muscle strength and physical performance. Journal of Cachexia, Sarcopenia and Muscle , 10 : 298 – 310 . 10.1002/jcsm.12394 . Introduction A physically active lifestyle attenuates the age‐related loss of muscle mass (i.e. sarcopenia) and associated decrements of muscle function 1 , 2 by increased muscle protein synthesis rates after exercise but also due to preservation of skeletal muscle sensitivity to dietary amino acids and suppressing the catabolic inflammatory cytokines in the muscle. 3 , 4 , 5 Sufficient protein intake is another vital component to maintain and regain muscle mass. 6 , 7 , 8 Current recommendations for adults advice 0.8 g/kg/day. 9 However, the PROT‐AGE study group suggested that older adults above 65 years of age should consume 1.0–1.2 g/kg/day to compensate for the attenuated capacity of protein utilization in the aging muscles. 6 For physically active older adults, their recommendation is even higher, i.e. ≥1.2 g/kg/day in order to comply with the synergistic effects of exercise and protein intake on muscle protein synthesis. 6 It has previously been shown that more than 50% of physically active older adults has a protein intake below 1.2 g/kg/day. 10 This observation suggests that physically active older adults may not consume enough protein to be utilized for the exercise‐induced improved muscle protein synthetic response and, thus, to prevent age‐related muscle mass loss. Therefore, we assessed the effects of 12 weeks of daily protein supplementation on lean body mass, muscle strength, and physical performance in physically active older adults with a low habitual protein intake. We hypothesized that protein supplementation in physically active older adults would induce beneficial effects on lean body mass, muscle strength, and physical performance, while no effects were expected in the control group receiving an iso‐caloric placebo.

extracted_data.document_summary: This study investigated the effects of 12 weeks of daily protein supplementation in physically active older adults with low habitual protein intake, who were also training for a multi-day walking event (Nijmegen Four Days Marches). Key findings revealed that protein supplementation led to a significantly larger increase in relative lean body mass and a greater reduction in fat mass compared to a placebo group. While both groups experienced improvements in physical performance (gait speed, chair-rise ability, Timed Up-and-Go test, and cardiorespiratory fitness), muscle strength and contractile function did not show significant between-group differences. Serum urea levels increased specifically in the protein group, reflecting higher protein intake, but most other biochemical markers for renal function and muscle damage showed no significant between-group differences, suggesting the intervention was safe.

treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial conducted over 12 weeks. Participants received a daily total of 31g of milk protein (divided into two 250mL servings: one at breakfast and one within 30 minutes after exercise; on non-exercising days, the second beverage was consumed during lunch) or an iso-caloric placebo. This increased the protein group's total daily protein intake from 0.86 ± 0.23 g/kg/day to 1.29 ± 0.28 g/kg/day. Both groups also engaged in walking exercise training as preparation for a 4-day walking event (30, 40, or 50 km/day). No dose-response comparisons were reported.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Relative lean body mass increased by 0.93 ± 1.22% in the protein group, which was significantly larger than the placebo group (∆0.44 ± 1.40%, P Interaction = 0.046).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Indicator of muscle and non-fat tissue mass, crucial for physical function and metabolic health.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: 12 weeks of daily 31g milk protein supplementation in physically active older adults with low habitual protein intake, performing moderate intensity walking exercise.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates a delay in age-related loss of muscle mass (sarcopenia), potentially preserving physical function and contributing to the health benefits of an active lifestyle.
analyzed_biomarkers.research_outlook: Future studies are warranted to assess possible sex-specific differences, as beneficial effects appeared more pronounced in women than in men.

analyzed_biomarkers.biomarker_name: Muscle strength (hand grip strength, isometric leg extension)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No significant differences in muscle strength (isometric leg extension and grip strength) were found over time between groups; no additional improvements found due to protein supplementation.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Ability of muscles to exert force, crucial for daily activities and preventing sarcopenia.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: 12 weeks of daily 31g milk protein supplementation in physically active older adults with low habitual protein intake, performing moderate intensity walking exercise.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: No additional benefits of protein supplementation on muscle strength observed in this population beyond the effects of physical activity alone.
analyzed_biomarkers.research_outlook: Further investigation (e.g., muscle biopsies) is needed to determine if muscular hypertrophy was myofibrillar or sarcoplasmic, which could explain the lack of strength improvements. Increased protein intake alone may not be sufficient without targeted resistance training.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No significant differences in quadriceps muscle contractile function were found over time between groups.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Characteristics and efficiency of muscle contraction, underpinning physical performance.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: 12 weeks of daily 31g milk protein supplementation in physically active older adults with low habitual protein intake, performing moderate intensity walking exercise.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: No additional benefits of protein supplementation on muscle contractile function observed in this population.
analyzed_biomarkers.research_outlook: Further investigation (e.g., muscle biopsies) is needed to understand the underlying cellular changes in muscle tissue that may explain the lack of functional improvements. May require more specific training stimuli than walking exercise.

analyzed_biomarkers.biomarker_name: Physical performance (Short Physical Performance Battery, Timed Up-and-Go test)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Gait speed, chair-rise ability, and Timed Up-and-Go improved in both groups (P < 0.001), but no significant between-group differences were observed, indicating protein supplementation had no additional impact on changes. Participants had high baseline physical performance scores.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Overall functional capacity related to daily activities and mobility, reflecting independence and quality of life.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: 12 weeks of daily 31g milk protein supplementation in physically active older adults with low habitual protein intake, performing moderate intensity walking exercise.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: The tests used (SPPB, TUG) were likely not sensitive enough for this high-functioning population, suggesting a ceiling effect and limiting the ability to detect additional protein supplementation benefits.
analyzed_biomarkers.research_outlook: Alternative tests, such as the 400m walk test, are recommended for future studies to adequately assess physical performance in high-functioning participants.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Cardiorespiratory fitness (Åstrand–Rhyming submaximal exercise test) improved in both groups (P < 0.001), but no significant between-group differences were observed.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Efficiency of the body's circulatory and respiratory systems to supply oxygen to muscles during sustained physical activity, important for endurance and overall health.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: 12 weeks of daily 31g milk protein supplementation in physically active older adults with low habitual protein intake, performing moderate intensity walking exercise.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Protein supplementation did not provide additional benefits to cardiorespiratory fitness in physically active older adults who already had a higher baseline VO2 max compared to populations in other studies.
analyzed_biomarkers.research_outlook: Untrained participants may benefit more from protein supplementation for improvement of aerobic fitness than already physically active older adults.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased in the protein group, whereas no changes were observed in the placebo group (P Interaction < 0.001).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: End-product of protein catabolism and indicator of nitrogen excretion; reflects protein metabolism and renal filtration.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: 12 weeks of daily 31g milk protein supplementation in physically active older adults training for the Nijmegen Four Days Marches.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates increased protein intake and metabolism, primarily reflecting a physiological response to higher protein consumption and higher nitrogen load. While consistently elevated levels can signal potential renal stress, within this context, it primarily reflects the physiological response to higher protein consumption.
analyzed_biomarkers.research_outlook: Future studies should assess long-term renal health implications of sustained elevated protein intake in older adults and investigate if these changes are accompanied by other markers of renal strain or are simply adaptive responses to increased protein load. Monitoring urea levels alongside other renal markers is recommended, particularly for individuals with pre-existing kidney conditions.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased after 12 weeks in both groups (P Time < 0.001), but no significant between-group differences were observed.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Waste product of muscle metabolism, used as an indicator of renal function.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: 12 weeks of daily protein/placebo supplementation in older adults training for the Nijmegen Four Days Marches, combined with walking exercise.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Increased levels typically indicate a decrease in kidney filtration rate, though can also be affected by muscle mass or intense exercise. Indicator of renal function.
analyzed_biomarkers.research_outlook: Further assess the clinical significance of this increase in the context of the intervention and overall health, especially for long-term protein supplementation.

analyzed_biomarkers.measured_tissue_or_fluid: Serum (Kidney function estimation derived from serum creatinine)
analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Clinical Marker Estimation/Renal Function Marker (Blood Parameter)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Decreased after 12 weeks in both groups (P Time < 0.001), but no significant between-group differences were observed. The study concludes that no significant differences were observed compared to the placebo group, suggesting the intervention was safe for renal function.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Indicator of kidney function, assessing the rate at which blood is filtered by the kidneys.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: 12 weeks of daily protein/placebo supplementation in physically active older adults with low habitual protein intake, combined with walking exercise.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Decreased eGFR indicates a decline in kidney filtering capacity, which can be a concern for renal health. However, the study's conclusion indicates that enhancing protein intake (to 1.29 g/kg/day) is a safe strategy for renal function in this population, given no between-group differences and stable albumin/creatinine ratio.
analyzed_biomarkers.research_outlook: Conduct follow-up studies to determine if the observed eGFR decrease is transient, related to exercise, or indicative of long-term renal impact, especially with sustained protein intake. While 24h urine creatinine is the gold standard, the combined assessment of serum eGFR and urinary albumin/creatinine ratio provides sufficient evidence that renal function was unaffected.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: No significant changes were seen over time in either group.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Indicator of kidney function, specifically detecting albuminuria which can signal kidney damage by assessing protein leakage.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: 12 weeks of daily 31g milk protein supplementation in physically active older adults with low habitual protein intake.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates that enhancing protein intake (to 1.29 g/kg/day) is a safe strategy for renal function in this population, as no signs of kidney damage (albuminuria) were observed.
analyzed_biomarkers.research_outlook: While 24h urine creatinine is the gold standard, the combined assessment of serum eGFR and urinary albumin/creatinine ratio provides sufficient evidence that renal function was unaffected.

analyzed_biomarkers.research_outlook: Investigate factors contributing to the increase in both groups (e.g., outdoor activity during walking exercise) and whether the baseline levels influenced outcomes.
